title: The body like a jar (40–43)
hookLine: the body is fragile as a jar; a well-directed mind does more good than mother or father (Dhammapada 43)

lines: A CLAY JAR FROM THE WELL.
cards: A clay water jar comes back from the well, full. Two things are true of it. It's useful every single day.
And one slip on a wet step, one knock against a doorframe, and it's gone. That doesn't make the jar worthless. It means carrying it with care: both hands, eyes on the step.
The Dhammapada holds the human body up beside that jar.

teach.b: Verse forty says: knowing the body is fragile like a jar, make the mind firm like a fortress, and meet Mara with the weapon of wisdom. Fragile body, firm mind.
Then verse forty-one, a stark one: “Before long, alas! this body will lie on the earth, despised, without understanding, like a useless log.” The commentary sets that verse in a moving scene.
A monk named Tissa fell ill with sores that covered his whole body. His robes stuck to him. The other monks couldn't bear it and left him alone.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA WASHES THE SICK MONK.
teach.b: The Buddha, seeing this, heated water himself, washed the sick monk with his own hands, and washed his robe and dried it in the sun. Then, while Tissa lay clean and comfortable, he spoke the verse.
So the verse about the log isn't contempt for the body. It comes from the one person who was willing to wash it. The body is fragile, and it deserves care; it just isn't the whole story.
Then the chapter turns. Verse forty-two says a wrongly directed mind does us more harm than any enemy.
And verse forty-three is its bright twin: “Not a mother, not a father will do so much, nor any other relative; a well-directed mind will do us greater service.” That's a big claim.
A good mother feeds, worries, teaches. The verse says your own mind, pointed well, can do even more, because it goes everywhere with you.
So chapter three closes where it began: straighten the arrow, guard the gate, and carry the jar with care.

how: Buddhists often reflect on the body's fragility as a way of loosening attachment, and the story of the Buddha washing the sick monk Tissa is told as a model of caring for the ill.

games.q: what does “the body like a jar” mean?
o: worthless, just a container to throw away
unbreakable if you keep it strong and fit
fragile and useful, so worth carrying with care

games.q: match the pieces of verses forty to forty-three.
p: does more than mother or father

s: the useless-log verse shows the Buddha despised the body
the commentary sets it right after he washed a sick monk with his own hands.
verse forty-three says a well-directed mind does more for us than mother or father
a striking claim, set beside the care of parents.
in the story, the other monks cared for the sick Tissa
they left him alone; the Buddha washed him and his robe himself.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a monk lies alone, covered in sores; the others have left him. what do you do?
o: send a monk to deal with it.
heat water and wash him and his robe yourself.
teach a sermon on impermanence first.
games.why: the commentary says he washed Tissa with his own hands, dried his robe in the sun, and only then spoke verse forty-one.

practice: If there's a cup or a mug near you, hold it in both hands; if not, imagine one, its weight, its smoothness, its edge, and know, not grimly, just clearly, that it can break.
Feel your own hands holding it the same way, warm, useful, fragile, and set it down gently. Then sit with the breath, and let the mind be firm and kind, like someone who knows how to carry a jar.

wordCard.voice: The body like a jar. Fragile, useful, and worth carrying with care, while the mind, pointed well, does more good than a mother or father.

orig.note: Pali: a water jar, the picture of the fragile body in verse forty.

carryVoice: Your line: more than a mother can. Fragile body, firm mind. That's day one hundred sixty-seven.
